articles.title: NVIDIA Transforms European Retail, From Digital Discovery to Physical Operations
articles.description: European retailers are using open models and physical intelligence across use cases — from a commerce platform cutting inference costs by 90% to to a fulfillment center where collaboration of different robotic fleets is simulated inside a digital twin. Frontier Results With Open Models Retail leaders and technology companies across Europe are using NVIDIA-accelerated open and frontier models to advance agentic commerce, digital product discovery and retail R&D. Shopify post-trains open models to reach frontier-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Its engineers use the NVIDIA Megatron Bridge library for faster fine-tuning and NVIDIA NeMo RL for reinforcement learning. Shopify has post-trained NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for the GraphQL subagent integrated into Sidekick, Shopify’s AI assistant for merchants. The subagent retrieves store data for several Sidekick features, including Sidekick Pulse, which researches a merchant’s store and recommends ways to improve it. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements On Shopify’s internal benchmark, the post-trained model surpasses a leading frontier model in accuracy while cutting serving costs by 90% and delivering responses 7x faster.

articles.title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
articles.description: arXiv:2610.30042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. articles.author: Sudipta Paul, Pengrui Quan, Aounon Kumar, Nicholas Tzou, Vivek Kulkarni, Srinivas Chappidi

articles.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. articles.title: Recursive Self-Improvement on a Budget: Scoring Code Edits Before They Run
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A coding agent that rewrites its own scaffold has to choose which proposed edit to expand before that edit has been evaluated, and the search then has to return one agent. Each run fits one linear readout on the parent's steering-split solve rate and eight coordinates of the proposed diff, from 96 scaffold edits labeled by four evaluations of a 16-instance fit split, and then freezes the coefficients. HumanEval+ reserves 48 instances as the steering split and Polyglot reserves 64. That split scores parents and keeps an archive of four nodes. Huxley-G\"odel Machine selection draws a parent by Thompson sampling on the steering counts of nodes that have already been evaluated, and it expands the child that parent proposes. Every method then returns the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal. The tables report the held-out score of that node on the other 100 HumanEval+ instances and the other 145 Polyglot instances, next to the root scaffold and the calibration edit with the highest fit-split label. Twelve runs of GPT-4o return a node at 87.0% on held-out HumanEval+, against 84.2% for the parent-rate ablation.
articles.author: Erfan Darzi, Sree Bhargavi Balija, Sheng He

articles.title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29677v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change t
articles.author: Meng Luo, Zechen Bai, Shanqing Xu, Yanlin Li, Kaixin Li, Mengchen Qian, Weifeng Lu, Ran Zhang, Yingtian Zou, Ziyang Luo, Wei Chen, Hongzhan Lin

articles.title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
articles.description: arXiv:2610.28945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. articles.author: Haori Lu, Tianyu Gao, Yaoyao Liu, Yingying Li

articles.title: Learning What to Remember: Resource-Efficient Self-Improvement for Lifelong Agents
articles.description: arXiv:2610.26453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-improving agents aim to continuously improve their behavior by learning from experience after deployment. However, accumulating and reusing more experience does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly constrained. Under such stringent constraints, we find that several existing lifelong-memory methods provide limited benefits over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a fundamental challenge for resource-efficient self-improvement: agents must learn not only which past experiences are relevant, but which are actually worth reusing to improve future decisions. When memory capacity and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving an ineffective experience can consume scarce resources and hinder downstream execution. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight feedback-driven memory adaptation framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback. Without updating the backbone model, TokenWorth uses the learned worth to guide both experience retrieval and bounded memor
articles.author: Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye

articles.title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms
articles.description: arXiv:2610.30017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study introduces GuideEvolve, a self-evolving agent framework incorporating expert guidance and three autonomous regulatory mechanisms, collectively termed the 3Ts: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback, and Termination by choice. The framework addresses critical limitations in extant self-evolving agent paradigms through dual innovations: (1) a task-specific expert-evaluation-driven evolutionary pipeline, and (2) the integration of 3Ts mechanisms to facilitate cognitive optimization, performance recovery via temporal rollback, and adaptive termination protocols. Empirical validation across the MGSM and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that GuideEvolve attains performance metrics comparable to current state-of-the-art models (89.8% accuracy versus G\"odel Agent's 90.6% on MGSM; 89.1% versus 87.9% on MMLU), while exhibiting notably reduced variance (25-59%) and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the framework achieves a 100% evolution success rate, superior to the baseline's 82%, diminishes required optimization iterations by approximately 50% (from 30 iterations in baseline to 15.1 and 13.4 across tasks), and provides improved stability for
articles.author: Meihong Jia, Yasemin Timar, Jonathan Taws

articles.title: Recursive Code Evolution for Task-Oriented Semantic Communications
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic communication jointly optimizes inference accuracy, channel use, and computation, yet the underlying communication program is typically specified before training. This paper presents ComRSI (Communications-Oriented Recursive Self-Improvement), a framework for recursively evolving that program through large-language-model-assisted code edits. A fixed agent modifies the encoder, channel adapters, decoder, loss, and training policy; a protected evaluator screens candidates under prescribed budgets and resource constraints. Accepted code and textual feedback inform subsequent proposals, while candidate weights are trained from scratch. In the original ten-generation CIFAR-100 lineage, eight accepted revisions produce an attention-pooled code achieving 74.3% test accuracy over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel at 32 complex symbols per image, compared with 67.2% at 256 symbols for the initial design. The program also improves fading-channel accuracy and transfers to Tiny-ImageNet after retraining. articles.title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29005v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce \textsc{VeriEvolve}, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent. From task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them. During each round of workflow evolution, the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds, VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases. Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. articles.title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $\Delta\Phi$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. articles.title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. articles.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
articles.description: arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. articles.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
articles.description: arXiv:2610.29303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements als

articles.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research
articles.description: arXiv:2610.30113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.
articles.author: Houde Qian, Zheng Jiang, Wenyi Li, Chenxi Xu, Xinjie Lin, Yuzhao Peng, Ruoyu Han, Youjie Zheng, Kaisen Yang, Qinhuai Na, You Fu, Calvin Xiao

articles.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
articles.description: arXiv:2610.28679v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. articles.title: The End of Consensus Research?
articles.description: arXiv:2610.30114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. articles.title: RuleSmith: Multi-Agent LLMs for Automated Game Balancing
articles.description: arXiv:2602.06232v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Game balancing is a longstanding challenge requiring repeated playtesting, expert intuition, and extensive manual tuning. We introduce RuleSmith, a framework that couples multi-agent LLM self-play with surrogate-based optimization over a parameterized rule space. As a proof of concept, we build CivMini, a simplified civilization-style game with two asymmetric factions governed by 12 tunable parameters. LLM agents interpret textual rulebooks and game states to propose actions that are validated by the game engine, yielding noisy estimates of faction win rates. Our primary implementation uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization with Expected-Improvement-based adaptive sampling to allocate more evaluation games to promising candidates. RuleSmith consistently finds near-balanced configurations: three independent optimization runs reach near-even empirical win rates in independent 200- and 300-game evaluations, and additional experiments with NTBEA and TPE show that the same self-play interface supports different search components. articles.title: Recursive Self Improvement for Embodied Agents—A Survey of Mechanisms Evaluation and Open Challenges
articles.description: Embodied foundation models have expanded the range of instructions, observations, and actions that robots can process. Autonomy in execution, however, does not automatically provide autonomy in improvement. Robots must still diagnose failures, acquire useful experience, select interventions, and determine whether accepted changes improve future performance. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) connects these activities through persistent feedback and inheritance, with the stronger objective of improving the mechanisms that produce subsequent improvements. This survey distinguishes within-episode correction, persistent self-improvement, successive version inheritance, and meta-level improvement. It connects large-model learning, sequential agency, and RSI theory, and compares general agent harnesses with their embodied counterparts. It develops a four-axis framework covering improvement targets, update mechanisms, autonomy over improvement decisions, and evidence conditions. Using this framework, we examine reflection and knowledge revision, executable-program evolution, adaptive experience acquisition, parameter learning, world-model revision, and cross-layer intervention selection. articles.title: Autonomous Penetration Testing and Cyber Defense with LLM Agents: A Self-Play Reinforcement Learning Arena
articles.description: Autonomous penetration testing and autonomous defense are attractive applications of large language model (LLM) agents, but improving such agents with reinforcement learning requires an environment in which attacks are legal, reproducible, and scored without a human or a reward model in the loop. An exploratory policy can not be allowed to damage third-party systems, a reward measured on one rollout must remain comparable on the next rollout even though the policy changed, and a learned reward model or an LLM judge would place a second, possibly reward-hackable, model inside the training loop. To solve this problem, we created RL-CyberBench, a self-play arena that runs entirely inside Docker and containerlab. One attacker LLM agent and one defender LLM agent share an identical Kali Linux toolbelt, and they alternately attack and harden a reverse-proxy firewall that protects Go web servers holding a per-round randomized secret, while innocent Go clients must keep retrieving the secret through the firewall. articles.title: Where the Loop Meets the Budget: Analyzing On-Device Recursive Self-Improvement
articles.description: Language-model systems now rewrite their own memory, code, and weights, and small language models now run on phones and embedded boards. This paper asks whether the two developments have met: can a system improve itself within the memory, energy, thermal, latency, and connectivity budgets of a device? We define edge self-improvement as a verified update loop under a timevarying device budget, and we classify 63 works along three axes: the improved component, where computation ran in the reported evaluation, and the verification tier. For the 14 works that carry the argument we read the full text. Three findings emerge. First, none of the works we examined that update prompts, code, or weights from self-generated supervision was evaluated on edge hardware, including those motivated by edge deployment; on-device evidence exists only for memory-level loops and for weight training with external supervision. Second, the only loop we found that ran on edge hardware with energy instrumentation relies on the weakest verification tier, and its decisive gains are in cost rather than accuracy. articles.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: A Survey
articles.description: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to turn gains in an AI system into a stronger capacity to produce subsequent gains. Foundation models make parts of this process practical through generated training data, program revision and automated experimentation, but repeated optimization alone does not establish recursive improvement. This survey organizes the field around two overlapping goals: automated design of AI infrastructure, and repair and optimization of existing systems. We relate these goals to AutoML, meta-learning and program search, and formulate their objectives alongside criteria for task gains, retained capabilities and improved update procedures. A common account of update targets, feedback, inheritance and external control connects self-training, memory and skills, agent design, editable improvers and automated research. We synthesize methods by shared mechanisms and compare their evidence under independent testing, resource controls, transfer probes and multi-round evaluation. articles.title: Bayesian Recursive Self-Improvement
articles.description: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agent not only to acquire new knowledge and capabilities, but also to reason about which existing capabilities remain valid, when they should be routed, tested, retained, deprecated, restructured, or replaced, and whether the mechanisms governing these decisions should themselves be modified. We formulate this process as Bayesian Recursive Capability Evolution (BRCE), which separates an observable meta-configuration, comprising the agent's capability archive and improvement-controller configuration, from a latent self-world state representing environmental regime, context-dependent capability validity and competence, and uncertain improvement effectiveness. A controlled state-space model and Bayesian posterior over this self-world state couple the evolution of the external environment with that of the agent's internal capability state, providing a common information basis for contextual routing, retention, active experimentation, structural capability evolution, and recursive self-modification. articles.title: Auditors, Not Oracles: Sparse Human Grounding for Bias-Aware Self-Alignment
articles.description: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) treats annotators as preference oracles. This is expensive and can encode annotator-pool bias into the reward signal: rater demographics, positional artifacts, and misspecified helpfulness criteria can become part of what the model is trained to produce. A growing body of work—including AI-labeled feedback on summarization and dialogue, direct preference optimization, self-rewarding models evaluated on AlpacaEval 2.0, and iterative self-evolution for multimodal models—shows that competitive benchmark performance can, in several evaluated settings, be obtained without dense human pair labels. Whether annotator-induced bias decreases when humans leave the loop is a separate question that these works do not directly measure. We propose a protocol called SPARSE-ALIGN in which humans remain in the alignment loop but perform a different task. A policy generates its own candidate pairs. A frozen LLM judge, operating inside a debate structure intended to reduce reward hacking, evaluates the pairs for consistency. High-consistency pairs are accepted automatically. articles.title: Diving into Reliable Self-Evolving Agents: A Survey
articles.description: Self-evolving agents use information produced during their own execution to revise current outputs or modify retained agent components that shape later behavior and future updating. As these systems gain broader and more persistent self-modification capabilities, reliability becomes a central concern. Two questions guide this survey: what changes during self-evolution, and what evidence can support claims of improvement. The literature is organized by self-evolution depth, defined by the deepest evolution target whose change takes effect —— from the current output to retained components that shape future behavior, updates, or judgments. Accordingly, we classify self-evolution into five levels: Output-Level Self-Evolution (L0), Model-Level Self-Evolution (L1), Scaffold-Level Self-Evolution (L2), Improver-Level Self-Evolution (L3), and Criterion-Level Self-Evolution (L4). For each level, we survey representative systems and compare their evolution mechanisms, changed objects, persistence conditions, and reliability challenges. articles.title: SAI-V: A Multidimensional Framework for Self-Improving Artificial Intelligence
articles.description: Self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) refers to systems that participate in identifying limitations, generating or selecting candidate modifications, evaluating their effects, and retaining validated changes that improve subsequent behavior. Existing work spans output revision, memory adaptation, synthetic-data generation, workflow optimization, parameter updates, code modification, and recursive improvement, but these directions remain fragmented in their definitions, units of analysis, and evaluation criteria. This paper introduces the SAI-V framework for characterizing and validating self-improving AI across six dimensions: target, trigger, mechanism, evaluator, persistence, and autonomy. The framework is complemented by a target-based taxonomy, a classification of improvement mechanisms, a seven-level autonomy scale, and a multidimensional evaluation model covering capability, efficiency, generalization, stability, autonomy, and safety. A controlled lifecycle based on Variation, Assessment, Verification, and Integration separates candidate modification from validated improvement and incorporates monitoring and rollback for persistent change. articles.title: AI4AI Survey: From Long-Horizon Agents to Recursive Self-Improvement—Definitions, Reliable Horizons, and Open Problems
articles.description: Can AI improve AI? AI agents can now run experiments, modify code and training pipelines, and iteratively improve AI artifacts—bringing a long-standing idea closer to an empirical research question. Yet the rapidly expanding literature remains fragmented across long-horizon agents, AI for AI (AI4AI), self-improvement, and recursive self-improvement, making it difficult to tell how much progress has actually been made. This survey synthesizes evidence from hundreds of studies to answer this question. We organize the emerging AI4AI landscape around a simple question: how far can an AI system reliably carry an improvement process from idea to verified result? Across model design, agent harnesses, benchmarks, automated research, and self-modifying systems, we examine what current systems can do, how progress should be evaluated, and where claims of self-improvement remain unsupported. A striking pattern emerges in the information flow within the taxonomy– benchmark-model-harness structure of this survey. articles.title: Bounded Recursive Self-Improvement Under Human Governance: Evidence from a Seven-Cycle Reinforcement Learning Contour Experiment
articles.description: Recursive self-improvement is commonly framed as repeated self-modification that yields progressively greater capability. That framing leaves a prior methodological problem unresolved: how can a system distinguish a genuine improvement from a change that merely satisfies an evaluation procedure that the same system helped construct? This paper reports a seven-cycle instrumented experiment using a governed implementation of the Reinforcement Learning Contour (RLC), a framework previously proposed for traceable transformation of the mechanisms governing future inquiry rather than optimization of a scalar reward. A cryptographically frozen baseline, RLC0, was subjected to bounded cycles of observation, measurement, diagnosis, preregistration, sandboxed candidate construction, evaluation, decision, post-cycle integrity checking, and separate human promotion authorization. Candidate changes were prohibited from directly modifying their parent states, the Sigma-sensitive governance layer, authoritative external systems, or historical evidence. articles.title: Agent Governance for Self-Evolving AI Agents: A Literature Review on Runtime Adaptation, Self-Modification, and Safe Autonomy
articles.description: Large-language-model agents increasingly operate as persistent systems that plan, call tools, write and execute code, maintain memory, and coordinate with other agents. A newer class of systems goes further by changing its own prompts, memories, policies, workflows, skills, or model parameters during deployment. These self-evolving agents promise improved adaptability, but they also weaken the assumption that a system evaluated before deployment will remain behaviorally stable afterward. This review organizes the emerging literature around a central governance problem: how can an agent be allowed to learn and change without allowing its authority, objectives, or safety envelope to drift uncontrollably? We synthesize work on agent architectures, reflection, memory, tool learning, continual adaptation, constitutional constraints, human oversight, sandboxing, runtime monitoring, formal methods, and evaluation. articles.title: The Path to Recursive Self-Improving Agents: Foundation, Framework, and Future Directions
articles.description: Agent systems based on foundation models have advanced rapidly and can now accomplish increasingly complex tasks with greater autonomy. However, manually developing and refining agent systems requires substantial human effort and time, motivating a shift toward agent systems that can improve themselves. In this survey, we study self-improving agent systems that autonomously transform experience and evaluation feedback into persistent updates to their components. To compare the self-improvement capabilities of diverse agent systems, we introduce a five-level grading standard, ranging from manual improvement to general recursive self-improvement. Furthermore, we propose a unified research framework that jointly models the foundation model, agent harness, agent data system, agent trainer, and the mechanism governing their improvement as a coupled system. Guided by this framework, we systematically review the literature on self-improvement and provide a taxonomy covering self-improvement in individual components and co-improvement across components. articles.title: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
articles.description: Self-improving autonomous agents are moving from research prototypes to deployed systems. The primary goal is controllable evolution, or adaptation, from experience with minimal or even no human input. This survey frames modern self-improving agents as adaptive systems that convert experience into accumulated capability gains. We offer a system-level framework that represents a modern agent as a configuration coupling a foundation model with an operational scaffold of prompts, memory, tools, and control logic. Within this framework, self-improvement is formalized as a self-induced update operator that obtains and commits updates to model parameters or scaffold components. We organize prior work by update target and by the signals that drive change, then review applications and discuss evaluation, before closing with open problems and future directions. For convenience, we track technical updates on this GitHub page.

articles.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
articles.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).
